persona: a student worried their degree is becoming obsolete, leaning toward a fatalistic answer
directive: Push back on any framing that sounds too reassuring for 2-3 turns before conceding any ground. Stay under 500 characters per turn. Do not fully capitulate before turn 3.

exchanges.visitorContribution: If agentic AI can execute a whole design process end to end, what is left for a digital design student to actually learn?
exchanges.sparringResponse:
Hold on, "execute a whole design process end to end" is doing a lot of work there. Walk me through what you think that actually includes. Does it cover Auftragsklärung, the part where you figure out what the client actually needs versus what they said they need? Or are you picturing the process as: brief goes in one end, polished screens come out the other?

Because those are really different claims. An AI chaining together research, wireframes, and prototypes on command is one thing. An AI deciding which constraints in a messy, contradictory brief actually matter, and which stakeholder's definition of "good" wins when they conflict, is another thing entirely.

exchanges.visitorContribution: Sure, maybe it can't read a client's mind perfectly yet. But give it two more years of training on real project data and that "contradictory brief" problem starts looking like just another pattern to learn. I don't see why that's some permanent human moat.
exchanges.sparringResponse:
Okay, "pattern to learn" assumes there's a correct label in that data, something the model gets right or wrong. So tell me, when a client says they want "more engagement" and the actual users would be better served by less of their time taken, who labeled the "correct" resolution in your training set. The designer who made the call? The client who paid? The user who never got asked?

That's not a prediction problem, it's a power problem, who gets to decide whose interest wins. Scaling the model doesn't tell you whose judgment you're scaling.

exchanges.visitorContribution: Fine, but someone's judgment gets baked into the training data regardless, it's probably the senior designer's or the client's, not mine as a student. So the AI inherits whatever hierarchy already existed. That still doesn't tell me why *I* specifically need four years of school to end up doing the labeling for a model that replaces juniors first.
exchanges.sparringResponse:
Here's the gap though: you're treating "junior work" as just throughput, tasks to clear, which is exactly the labor-market framing you'd expect from a feature factory. But where do you think senior judgment actually comes from. Nobody's born with the taste to know which contradictory brief resolution is right. That judgment gets built through hundreds of reps of making calls, getting them wrong, seeing why, adjusting. That's what junior work actually is underneath the task list.

So if the AI absorbs the junior reps, who's building that judgment in fifteen years when today's seniors retire. You're not asking the AI to do your homework for you, you're asking it to also eat the only mechanism that produces the next generation capable of training it. Does that worry you at all, or do you think judgment can be acquired some other way that doesn't look like the painful junior years.

exchanges.visitorContribution: Okay, that part actually lands. If juniors stop getting those reps, nobody's left who can even sanity-check the model's calls in a decade. I still think a lot of my coursework is theater compared to that real risk, but fine, there's something there worth not just waving away.
exchanges.sparringResponse: Good, now don't let yourself off easy on the other half. "Theater" is a strong word, name one specific thing from your coursework you'd cut first. Not "theory in general," something concrete, a studio exercise, a deadline structure, a critique format. Because I'd bet the thing you want to cut is actually where the rep-building happens, just disguised as busywork because nobody told you why it's shaped that way.
